utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody and good morning to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Do you have any preliminaries? None. For the record, yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. I would just like to introduce John Karis. He's an intern with us from the United States, and he's sitting in with us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek and welcome, Mr. Karis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, it's a privilege to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record all the accused are here. I notice the absence of Mr. Haynes, Mr. Bourgon, from the Defence teams. Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls and Mr. Mitchell. All right. No preliminaries? I suppose we can bring in the witness and finish with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Krajisnik. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls is going to proceed with his cross-examination, after which I suppose we can send you back, and I'll make sure that the segregation order is lifted. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to start off today with a just a couple more questions about the 16th Assembly session. Yesterday, at transcript reference 21584, you stated that the 16th Assembly session was held in public. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that all the sessions were public so I suppose that one was as well. Now that I think about it, at one point, it may have been a closed session. It might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, let me help refresh your memory on that. If we could have 65 ter P25 up, please? On page 22 of the English, which is B/C/S 19. While waiting for that I'm going to ask you a question about what Dragan Kalinic said. He was Minister of Health; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. After the -- you introduce him on page 22 of the English, I won't read it all but he makes a speech about whether the war option or the option of negotiation should be chosen. And he says: "I say this with a reason, I must instantly add that knowing who our enemy is, how perfidious they are and how they cannot be trusted until they are physically militarily destroyed, and crushed, which of course implies eliminating and liquidating their key people, I do not hesitate in selecting the first option. The option of war. Because I believe that our fate, the fate of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina," he goes on to say he does not link it to the fate of Serbia Montenegro, has to be solved and cannot be solved in any other way but by war, and he continues to say, "Why do I say the war option seems more certain? Because only what has been conquered militarily can be really and truly ours." Now, that's not ordinarily the sort of topic I would think that would be discussed in a public gallery. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain why Mr. Kalinic said that. In my view, when I was listening to this, and while I said that there were not just assemblymen, I apologise, did you perhaps want to interrupt me here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just wanted to make you understand my question. I wasn't asking you to interpret what he said but whether that would be ordinarily said in public, a discussion of whether we should choose the war option and liquidate the other sides' leaders. Is that normally the kind of thing that would be said in public, just so you understand my question.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, everything people said, they would say it in public because they were embittered, the war had started, they were in panic and under the influence of what was going on around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's go to the next page which is page B/C/S, page 20 in the B/C/S, page 23 in the English. And here, Mr. Kalinic says: "Also I do not fully understand fully this statement, and I want it to be clarified here in this assembly, what would the proclamation of a unilateral cease-fire mean for us? The reason stated was that by doing this we would demonstrate to Europe that we were in favour of negotiations and a peaceful solution, but please since we are in a closed session of the assembly let me make it clear," and he continues to talk about the military solution. Reading that, does that remind you that this session was indeed private? Was not open to the public?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Galic's discussion is here as well. That's why I said that there were other people present, other than just the assemblymen but now that you have read this out, yes, I believe that at one point, the session was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Mr. Galic, you're referring to Colonel Galic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Captain Garic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there by chance, and on the terrace I remember it well, there were a lot of people present, as well as in the meeting room. I suppose that the record is correct. I don't know, and I can't believe that somebody would have put it in incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you a question now, moving on, about the map that we saw yesterday. And let me make it clear I'm asking you just a very technical point about the exhibits. And you'll see what -- I just want to clarify something that might have been unclear yesterday. Mr. Zivanovic showed you yesterday 1D1156, the statement of principles and maybe we could have that up. This is the 18 March Sarajevo statement of principles which concludes "this paper is the basis for further negotiations. All right. And could we just scroll through the pages which are in that exhibit in English, one by one? Actually, I can speed this up. There is one page from this packet missing, in the English ERN range is 02093996 through 02094001. And what we've got submitted is missing 0209400. Could I have 65 ter 3324 up now, please? Is that what we have up now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 65 ter 3324. I'm told it is in e-court. I can put it on the ELMO, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We couldn't find it either here so there must be something wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm told it now might be appearing in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, we have no such exhibit on the list which the Prosecution provided for cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can explain that. As I said, Mr. Zivanovic put in this statement of principles, Cutileiro Plan, and omitted one page of the ERN range, the map, and he asked about that map yesterday in his direct examination and said I'm not going to ask you about that map; and frankly I hadn't noticed that one page had been pulled out of the range when I originally got his exhibit so I want to show the witness that map just to confirm and for Your Honours that this is the map that was spoken of that was attached to the plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that satisfy you, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not that map. It is not the same map. I have nothing to show to the witness, the map I showed him but not another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The map you showed him was another map definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is what precisely trying to clarify for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, here, 02093996 we have the cover page which has Mr. Cutileiro's name on it, if we could go to the next page, 02093997 the first page of the statement of principles, if we could go to the next page. 02093998. Can we go to the next page? 02093999. And if we scroll down a bit, this is the last page of the statement of principles, it states it's the basis for further negotiations, Sarajevo, 18 March, 1992, one question, this is the so-called Sarajevo Agreement, correct? You need to answer orally?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the Sarajevo Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. 02094000, the next page. Can you just look at that, sir, see if you remember, if you can confirm that this is the map that was attached and was referred to as being attached to the statement of principles?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the map that was drawn on the 18th of March and was attached to the principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And just to round it out the end of the package, next page, 02094001, that is the section entitled, "Human rights," correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then just as you stated yesterday, we don't need to put it up but the map which Mr. Zivanovic showed you was from sometime in May 1992, from Lisbon, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's -- I'm done with that topic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may explain, please, I'm afraid that there has been a misunderstanding and that the misunderstanding remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you feel the need to explain further, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The map that has just been shown to me by the Prosecutor is the map which depicted Serb, Muslim and Croat municipalities with absolute and relative majorities according to the 1971, 1981 or 1991 census, and this is the map that was provided on the 18th of March. The map that was shown to me yesterday by Mr. Zivanovic is the map that was drawn after the meeting that we had on the eve of the 16th session. To prove that this is correct, please refer to the minutes of the meeting to see that Karadzic and Vjestica mentioned that at the last meeting, Europe had accepted the border on the Una. The map that we have just seen today, you can see that the border is not on the Una River, and on the map that Mr. Zivanovic showed to me yesterday, the border is on the Una River, in the western part of the state, and because this had been accepted by Europe, we incorporated that into one of our strategic goals so both maps are correct and what the Prosecutor said today, he is correct, but with the agreement reached on the 18th of March there was another map that was work in progress and we continued working on it during the negotiations and there were two other conferences after that. Thank you very much for allowing me the time to explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Let's clarify something else for that matter. Do I understand you well that apart from this map that you have just been shown today, there was another map attached to the same report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which was drawn at the last session on the eve of the 12th of May, from which we had come to this session, and that is the map shown to me yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But the map that you were shown yesterday, who drew up that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, the representatives of the Cutileiro Plan, as far as I can remember the name, the gentleman was Mr. Darvin. He drew up the map, he offered it to us for inspection and that map was published in various publications. Actually I can give you a publication where this map was published. I have it on me here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm asking you because that was in Cyrillic and also had in caption also Sarajevo singled out separate from the rest and the order of presentation was also different. You had Serbian first, Croatian second, Muslim third, and then Sarajevo while this one Sarajevo is missing and the order is reversed. You have the Muslim first and so on and so forth. So this is why I'm asking you because the two seem to be to me at least to be somewhat different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be given the time to explain this further, also?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, Mr. Krajisnik. You are here to answer questions and explain whatever needs explaining. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The map that Mr. Zivanovic showed to me yesterday, and which was preliminary drawn up in Lisbon, depicted Sarajevo as a place under the three-year or five-year protectorate of the United Nations and that is why it is marked and only the municipality of Pale shown separately. After that time, Sarajevo would have been internally divided. The rest of the Sarajevo would be split, one-third would go to the Serb side, and the other two-thirds would go to the Serbs and to the Croats. The city had its administration and that is one -- why one of our goals says that we wanted a part of Sarajevo that would belong to Republika Srpska. That's why in this map it is marked separately and you will see that in all the subsequent agreements that Sarajevo is especially marked and there was a special agreement on the divided city of Sarajevo. And there should have always been a temporary solution until the final internal demarcation, it should have been only internal because nobody really wanted to split up Sarajevo as a city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One last question on this: 1D1159, the map in Cyrillic from the Lisbon talks, the Muslim side never agreed to this map at Lisbon, did they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Serb side did not agree either. This was a map which was still work in progress which called for further work but some things were agreed upon and it was the proposal of the international community to us to continue working on this map. So you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. I'm done with the map. I would now like to go through a few more military documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have 1D1159?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe that's the number for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We couldn't see it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was wrong number, Your Honours. It's 1160.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I may have written the wrong number. I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the map I showed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, we couldn't find it at the time and we put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 3253?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, what's going to come up before you is a 1 KK, 1st Krajina Corps command document dated the 21st of May 1992. It's signed by the assistant commander for morale, Vukelic, and you've seen this document before and been asked about it before in your trial. If we can go directly to page 2 in the English, if we scroll down I can tell whether -- that's in paragraph 2 of the B/C/S. It should be there on the bottom of the page for you. I'm going to read out the same part that was read out to you in your trial. "The constituent Serbian people who live on around 65 per cent of the area and represent more than 35 per cent of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina must struggle for complete separation from the Muslims and Croatian people and form their own state. Only after that will they be able to decide with whom and how they will unite and associate." If we see on the last page of both English and B/C/S, at the bottom, one page earlier on the B/C/S, please, it says at the very end, "Inform all members of the army about this report in the most suitable way." And at the bottom which is on the next page now, sorry, "Send to all corps units." You were asked about this document on your trial on the 12th of June 2006, transcript 25554 to 25556. The same section was read out to you and you were asked if that was a reference to strategic goal -- strategic objective number 1 and you said: "This is information, Mr. Prosecutor, and this was in the strategic objectives but he's not referring to the strategic objectives rather he's referring to our general objectives. However, it is, yes, found in the first strategic objectives. However, this is information for the units. It's not an order." And a little bit further down you say, "However, a link can be established with the first strategic goal, I agree." Do you stand by that answer, that a link can be established between this document and the first strategic goal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what I said at my trial. I forgot. But I can explain the background of this statement which may shed some light on things, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You can explain it, of course, but I'm just asking, I've read out your answer, I can show you the transcript in English, if you need it, but do you want to change your answer or do you stick by that same answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, I don't have my whole transcript, and it's very difficult for me to explain based on just one segment. I can provide further explanation, and if the two don't tally, you may say that I'm not consistent, and that's that. I can't give you my answer based on just this one segment. I have not had the whole transcript after my trial. But let me tell you why this could be logical, why this could make some sort of sense, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Then the question is, just so you know, you can answer it without reference to your sic-ing, do you agree there was a link between what Vukelic wrote in this document and the first strategic objective?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Vukelic was not authorised to inform anybody about the six strategic goals and if he did it, he did it in the way he understood this. However, he was neither authorised nor instructed. He could have done it only after the 9th of July when this was made public and when the map was published. Before that he could have said whatever he wanted to say based on how he understood things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, it's not okay, Mr. Nicholls. Do I take your answer, it's a kind of an oblique answer you answered the question at a tangents more or less. Am I right in understanding your question as indirectly agreeing with what was proposed to you by the Prosecution? Namely that rightly or wrongly, in this document, Mr. Vukelic, what Mr. Vukelic is saying constitutes a link with the first strategic objective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you will allow me just to say a few sentences before I answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the negotiations, under the auspices of the international community, there were different proposals as to how to solve the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina. One of the proposals that was tabled was a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can provide you with that paper. In his book Mr. Owen said it ever so nicely. So there were various combinations at steak. In the Cutileiro Plan our position was the position of a compromise. Bosnia and Herzegovina was to be decentralised, three constituent units would be defined according to the geographic, ethnic and other principles. What Mr. Vukelic interpreted, based on what he had heard at the assembly session, that is his view, which he certainly must have based on the strategic goals, but this is not a correct interpretation. He was not authorised to provide any interpretations for that matter. That is my answer. I can provide you with a paper to show you that a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina was always on the table as one of the options.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear enough. Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 65 ter 3308, please. This is a Main Staff of the army of the RS strictly confidential, extremely urgent, directive for further actions, from the 6th of June 1992, and it's signed by General Mladic. This is another document you've seen before. This is less than a month after the 16th Assembly session. I want to recall what strategic goal 2 was, as printed, set up a corridor between Semberija and Krajina. I'd like to look now at page 2 of the document, and it's page 2 in both English and B/C/S. Under the heading, "The goal of the action," paragraph B. "Ensure contact between Semberija and Bosnian Krajina. Reject enemy forces farther away from the road, communication, and make it possible for normal traffic to take place." I'll read one more section to you before I ask you a question. If we turn to the next page, in the English, it's still the -- we can scroll down on the B/C/S, here, General Mladic is talking about the stages of the operation of the directive. "In the second stage, in duration of four to six days, create the corridor between Semberija and Bosnian Krajina." And it continues: "To extend the corridor permanently." That is strategic goal 2, almost verbatim, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not a strategic goal. This is a military goal which was brought about by the death of the 12 babies in Banja Luka. The military did this irrespective of strategic goals. We had agreed upon the strategic goal 2 with the Croatian side in Graz. There is a paper showing how to do it by political means. That was what was incorporated into our strategic goals. I can provide you with a document that reflects that agreement. And this was a move that had been forced by the interrupted communications between Semberija and Krajina as a result of which 12 babies died in Banja Luka and the military wanted to deal with that with military terms but that had nothing to do with our political goals, the political goals that had been agreed upon by -- with the other side in Graz, as I've told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So the goal as you a say is exactly the same but you're saying they are completely?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's a coincidence, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't want to comment. It's not my right to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll move on. 3254. We are going back to Bosanska Krupa, to talk about that a little bit. I want to read this entire short document. This is from the War Presidency of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa. On the 22nd of May 1992. It's an order issued by the president of the War Presidency, Gojko Klickovic. And I'm sure you remember but keep in mind what Mr. Vjestica said 10 days earlier in Banja Luka, at the 16th Assembly session. The order states, "To evacuate the remaining Muslim population from the territory of the Serbian municipality Bosanska Krupa." And then it goes on to state that it needs to be executed by 8.00 on the 24th of May. In your trial you referred to other orders as orders for ethnic cleansing. Is this an order for ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this order. There were no communications between us. I don't know whether this evacuation is about an offer for somebody to go somewhere or whether people had been expelled. You should ask Mr. Klickovic or Mr. Vjestica. Mr. Klickovic is currently on trial in Sarajevo for war crimes. I really wouldn't be able to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He's currently on trial for war crimes in Bosanska Krupa, correct? Murder, torture, forcible displacement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, I've helped you there. I've helped you understand. Didn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Actually, I already knew he was on trial for these crimes, in the state court in Bosnia, correct? You need to answer verbally. You nodded your head but could you please say yes or no verbally?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's in Sarajevo actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this is the municipality where, as Mr. Vjestica said and you agreed with me yesterday, Serbs were 24 per cent of the population, correct? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But they had 75 per cent of the territory of the municipality, and they made up 25 per cent of the total population, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You say there was no communication, but 10 days earlier, Mr. Vjestica addressed the entire assembly and said let me report to you, the assembly, on what's happening in Krupa, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But yesterday I wanted to explain things, but you wouldn't let me tell you why he said what he did, and further on, what he said in the statement provided to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber may give you the opportunity to say that. The reason I did not want you to explain that is because I'm not interested in his explanation for what he said. I was interested in the record of what he said at the assembly. Just so you understand. Could we go to the next document, 3255?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, but such answer might be misleading. I would like to give the witness opportunity to explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it's entirely in Your Honour's hands. My questions were about what Mr. Vjestica said at the assembly session. I'm not particularly interested in Mr. Vjestica's explanation for why he said those things because I'm sure that he -- I'm just not interested in that. Or the witness's interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Your Honours, sorry, that could be a matter for redirect if he wants to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's precisely what we are discussing, but at the same time, if that would be the only question on redirect, we might as well deal with it now and avoid the redirect. Mr. Krajisnik, rather, Mr. Zivanovic first, as things are at the moment, do you plan a redirect or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then we leave it for the redirect. You can ask Mr. Krajisnik the question. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to 3258, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 3258, actually. This is a related document I'd like to go through with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we have the wrong one, 3255, in fact, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, from the War Presidency of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanska Krupa, 25th of May 1992, so the day after the deadline in the order we just looked at expired. This is now a proposal rather than order. It's headed, by president of the War Presidency, Gojko Klickovic. And it's to the command of the 1st Podgrmec Brigade in Serbian Jasenica. One, of the proposal to carry outs all military preparations concerning the cleansing of the left bank of the Una River, including the right bank of the Una in the action in the area above Bosanska Otoka. Two, in course of preparations and cleansing of the left bank of the Una, destroy and pull down as many residential and other buildings as possible including demolishing of tunnels setting the pine wood in Tecija area on fire, and cleaning up the Kalender canal. Prepare the troops to hold on to the left bank of the Una for as long as it takes to withdraw material, if any, until the bridges in Bosanska Krupa and Bosanska Otoka have been prepared to be blown up, until the right bank of the Una has been fortified in a better way. If you recall, Mr. Vjestica's speech at the 16th Assembly session, he said, "And now we are preparing for Bosanska Otoka. God willing in 2 to 3 days we shall mine the bridge in Bosanska Otoka."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry for that, but we needed to discuss something, Mr. Nicholls. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's correct, in his report, Mr. Vjestica talked about the plan to blow up or mine this bridge, correct? In his report to the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vjestica explained it all to you, in the interview he gave you. I have nothing to do with it. I can only explain how I understood his words at the assembly as he confirmed in his interview subsequently. That has nothing to do with the six strategic goals. He himself said that they had done all that before the six strategic goals were put in place, well not this one, this one came later, it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And I don't want to go over it again but he did refer to the happy news that the Una was going to be the border, correct? In the 16th Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in the interview he said he boasted about it. He wanted to become more popular.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He boasted that the Muslims, he did not think, would be returning. Now, let's go to the reasons for this proposal. The first one, political determination to have the border of Serbian municipality autonomous region Banja Luka, Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbian state established along the river Una up to Bosanska Otoka. Strategic objective 4, as printed in the gazette, as discussed in the assembly session, establish a border at the Una and Neretva rivers. Mr. Klickovic is citing strategic objective 4 as one of the reasons for this proposal, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You see, we had agreed the Una as the border as early as Lisbon. It was before the strategic goals. And it was also decided that that should be resolved by political means rather than military means. That was also in the presentation of Mr. Karadzic. That's why we stated the Una was the border of our future maps. And of course this person mentioned it. I don't know why but he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So is that another coincidence, he's mentioning the exact language of strategic objective 4, 13 days later?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment. I can neither confirm nor deny. I don't know what Mr. Klickovic said. He probably was informed that it was politically agreed that the future border would be along the Una and then he made use of it the way he saw fit. He probably knew about it because Mr. Vjestica was at the assembly. He probably knew that it had been agreed that the map would be such that the border would go along the Una. That was supposed to be the political solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And he's got that -- sorry, not to continue on this too long -- as the reason to evacuate, cleanse, the area.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say again what Mr. Vjestica told you in his interview. He said they wanted to leave, we did not expel them. We helped them leave for their own security. That's what he told you. And I can merely repeat it to you. And that was the way I interpreted his words at the assembly. As to whether it was indeed so, only he can know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's go to 3258. 28th of May 1992, brigade command Birac, order to the Zvornik Territorial Defence Staff. Now 16 days after the assembly session. Signed by commander Svetozar Andric. I'm interested in paragraph 6. "The moving out of the Muslim population must be organised and coordinated with the municipalities through which the moving is carried out. Only women and children can move out while men fit for military service are to be placed in camps for exchange." Now, in your trial, they found that putting people, men, in camps was one of the methods of cleansing. Do you agree that putting people in these camps as we see in this order here was a way of cleansing them out of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is incriminating. It was something that my Major Andric ordered without having considered the consequences. One needs to bear in mind that in the header, it says, "Command of the Brigade of the Serb army" which as such did not exist. Then you have Birac and then up the military post of the former JNA. He sent this to the TO staff in Zvornik which by that time did not exist, since the army had been formed at the time. This is all very confusing. He was trying to find his way through the situation. Maybe he could explain to you better what he was trying to do. But of course it was impermissible to arrest and detain anyone without a need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And doesn't that also, this order, the goal in this order of removing the population from Zvornik, fit in with strategic goals 1 and 3?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has absolutely nothing to do with it. That man was in the region. He wasn't familiar with the strategic goals, and I don't think he could have referred to them. This is how we -- how he acted locally. He was engaged by the region. There is another order that we didn't see here. In any case, this does not have anything to do with the six strategic goals and I stated that at my trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 3261. This is a 2nd of June 1 KK report to the Main Staff of the VRS. Paragraph 2 at the bottom, it's a regular combat report, by the way, signed for General Talic, the 1 KK commander. And it states: "In the area of Derventa there continues to be occasional artillery fire while because the Muslim extremists have failed to hand in their weapons, the Muslim population of the area of Lisnja village has been expelled." Now, the Trial Chamber in your case found that you had demanded that new ethnic facts be created on the ground. It's para 1076. This document reflects in Lisnja the creation of those new ethnic facts, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you base your qualifications upon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, the documents we have been looking at. I know it began earlier. But this is another document showing, as the others we've seen, showing the expulsion of the Muslim population, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Lisnja is in the municipality of Prnjavor. Mr. Nemanja Vasic municipal president, testified. He explained the entire process. He said that he returned the Muslims to Lisnja so that they wouldn't leave. He said that they were not expelled. The problem was resolved and that he did not notify any of us from the leadership concerning the process. It took place locally, following the request of the Muslims. In his words, there was no expulsion, and it had nothing to do with the six strategic objectives, that's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we are not going to retry all the expulsions from the ARK but then, just so I understand you, you don't have to keep saying it, are you saying that in each of these instances the Muslims left on their own accord out of fear and they were helped by the local SDS authorities? Is that what you claim?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am stating that the way the Muslim expulsion from the territory of Republika Srpska was qualified is to say the least not completely true. And I can explain further what information I base this on. I stated this in my appeal. If you're interested to hear, I'll explain why it isn't true that the Muslims were all expelled from Republika Srpska, as they would have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While we are briefly on Prnjavor, did you personally know Veljko Milankovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't personally know Veljko Milankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we have time we will look at documents about him later but do you agree with me he was a criminal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It requires clarification, what does it mean, criminal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I mean I understand the word criminal but maybe you need to explain further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can rephrase it to make my friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Someone with a criminal record?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that Veljko Milankovic led a paramilitary group called the Wolves of Vucjak? In the early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milankovic, the late Mr. Milankovic, led the Wolves of Vucjak which at first was an independent unit and later became part of the 1st Krajina Corps. You are correct. He commanded the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that when he commanded the unit, let's talk now about just when it was independent, that it committed crimes which I'll define as shooting at, blowing up buildings, harassing the Muslim population of Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the issue. I know what you are getting at. And I'll explain. At a certain moment, I commended Milankovic. I think you're getting at that. I can explain why it was done. It is my opinion now that he was a criminal, that we weren't able to control him, and I can explain what my reasons were to hold the opinion I did at the time and why I'm holding this opinion now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, just let me break that up a bit and you can explain. You agree with me that when he was the leader of the paramilitary unit, he engaged in criminal acts against the Muslim population? Just yes or no. Do you agree with that? And then you can explain why you praised him.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that he committed -- that he was a criminal, but I can state that he committed criminal acts and that he was harassing Muslims, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, explain, if you want to, why you praised that man.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, I believe, I was at a gathering in Prnjavor. It was then that the local authorities, to whom Mr. Milankovic was a hero and a positive character, talked to me about him as someone who had been a hero and was killed defending the Serbian people, and at that pre-election gathering, I praised Mr. Milankovic and his unit. From the documents I saw later, I realised that before the war he had a criminal record, that he had served sentences, and that he also had a special unit which in a way created chaos in town, shooting, harassing Muslims. As for any other criminal acts, I don't know whether he committed any. By virtue of Mr. Galic's [as interpreted] order, that unit became a regular unit of the 1st Krajina Corps. That's the truth why I behaved the way I did and why today, after all the information I saw, I believe that he was so to say a person who was in conflict with law before and during the war. And that was the position he entered the war from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, as you say, make it clear, he was a hero to the local authorities in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what they told me, and they still hold that opinion. Almost 90 per cent of his unit was killed in action and that is how people see those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 3262, please? I'll do this very quickly. This is a document you've seen before. Sanski Most Crisis Staff, conclusions from the 4th of June 1992. And the conclusions are formed by Nedeljko Rasula, who was president of the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most and also of the War Presidency. Colonel Nedjo Anicic, Sanski Most TO. And we also see references to having a talk with Colonel Stevilovic from the 1st Krajina Corps. The conclusions in 1 are that Mirko Vrucinic, I believe was the vice-president of the Crisis Staff, Nedeljko Rasula and Nedjo Anicic shall be in charge of resolving the issue of prisoners and their categorisation and deportation to Manjaca. Let's look quickly at the categories. One, politicians, 2, nationalist extremists, 3, people unwelcome in Sanski Most municipality. First, do you agree with me that Manjaca camp was a VRS prison camp?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly need to object. I don't know why I need to answer such questions. I explained all that in my trial, and this shouldn't be another trial for me. It is a well known fact that Manjaca was a military prison, but I didn't know at the time that it existed or anything else for that matter. As for these conclusion, when it was discussed, I said I wasn't privy to it and why it was done. It has nothing to do with the six strategic objectives and with the gist of the testimony I was supposed to provide here. If the goal is to use this testimony to my detriment in my appeal, I have to ask the Chamber to relieve me of the need to voluntarily answer these questions. However, I will do so if I am ordered by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it was a very simple question. You made it sound complicated and complicated it further. It was simple question asking you do you agree that Manjaca camp was a VRS prison camp? And you should have answered either yes or no. Irrespective of whether you came to know about that at the time or later. If you need to explain that, of course you have a right to. Otherwise, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, I am not objecting to this question alone but rather to all the questions which are beyond the scope of the six strategic objectives. If it is necessary for me to explain what my view of ethnic cleansing is, I will do so. As for the rest, I object because I see this as an attempt to harm me in my appeal proceedings. I've already answered that to my knowledge Manjaca was a military camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Let me just consult with my colleagues on one thing and then we continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. How much more do you have, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Actually, I think I would -- I have some more -- I have probably another -- I would finish sometime next session. I can move it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then this is our suggestion to you. Please try to move it up because we are wondering and wandering in a territory that may have much less importance than all of you might think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, if you give me one moment, Your Honours. All right. I'll skip ahead a little bit and go to P29, directive 4. This is the 19th of November 1992, if we could go to, we have seen this before so I won't go through it much. Go to page 5 in the English. Apparently it's page 11 on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Something you were asked about in your trial. It states, "The Drina Corps from its present position, under paragraph D, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad, the dam, Zvornik and the corridor while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region so exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population." Now, just very quickly, you discussed this order in your trial and in a question -- and you agreed that this language was an order for ethnic cleansing, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I do not understand why Mr. Mladic wrote this because it's not what I heard from him. I also said that before this directive, on the 17th of October, and in December, I provided two statements in which I firmly stood against ethnic cleansing. That is my full answer. As for this being permissible or whether it is ethnic cleansing, one could interpret it that way, of course. Why would the population leave, if there was no other reason for them to leave? Why should they leave if their army left? However, I'm no soldier and I don't know why this would be logical. You need a professional to resolve this. I can only comment upon this in lay terms. I was rather surprised to see this as part of this directive, and I was also able to read it here in this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. 65 ter number 3307. This is the 53rd session of the RS Assembly from 20th August 1995. I'd ask to go to page 68 of the English, B/C/S page 87.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me where this session was held?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Jahorina Pale.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you -- on the second page it says that you were the chairman. I want to read out to you one part of something Mr. Karadzic said at this assembly session. Again, August 1995. "We absolutely cannot let ourselves get any ideas about them taking our traditional territories from us. To tell the truth, there are towns that we've grabbed for ourselves and there were only 30 per cent of us. I can name as many of those as you want but we cannot give up the towns where we made up 70 per cent. Don't let this get around, but remember how many of us there were in Bratunac, how many in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how many in Rogatica."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you help me find the passage?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Page 68 of the English -- 69 of the English, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the reason I don't think we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, it splits over. It should be at the top of page 69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, all right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My screen should be moved as well. I don't have that part of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll just finish quickly. "How many in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how many in Rogatica, how many in Vlasenica, in Zvornik, et cetera. Due to strategic importance they had to become ours and no one is practically questioning it any more." Now, he's talking there about these towns along the Drina, a thing of strategic importance, is that related to strategic goal 3 or is it coincidental?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not coincidental, but it's not the third strategic objective either. 430.000 Serbs left the federation for Republika Srpska. And 430.000 Muslims went the other way. Mr. Karadzic says, "We are now losing the territory where there -- where we were in majority, holding on to the towns where we were in minority." And now no one is questioning that. Traditionally speaking we had the majorities in certain areas, and now it was on the other side. This probably had to do with the contact group plan. That is why he was talking about it, trying to persuade the deputies and to explain to them why not all of their towns can be in the map itself. He was trying to explain the principles of win some, lose some. This was probably a part of a plan, but I cannot see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Win some, lose some. And the win he's talking about there, just the plain meaning --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was discussing the map, and what we gained and what we lost. You can find the agenda. Probably you'll see a reference to the contact group plan. Here he's saying, "We were in the minority here and we hold that territory. And on this part we were in the majority, and we don't have it." That's why he's trying to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. But isn't he also talking in the very plain meaning where he says grabbed about these towns, where Serbs, as he said, were in a minority, they have now been taken and it's a fact that he's not going to change, they have been grabbed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a document which is a very long document. I think the Prosecutor is saying something and the witness is saying something else. I don't think one could take this sentence from the context. Maybe we should have a hard copy and give a hard copy to the witness to know exactly what is in the document. Because I don't believe we'll manage to find our way in all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Do you wish to comment or proceed with your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. This is -- this is -- I just wanted you to comment on this statement which was put forward in this trial as a quote basic fact. On April 8th, 2007, an attack was conducted on Zvornik. Many units were involved in this attack including units of the Zvornik Territorial Defence which were commanded by Branko Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the date is wrong. It is page 31, line 17. The year is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, yes, on April 8, 1992 an attack was conducted on Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Many units were involved in this attack including units of the Zvornik Territorial Defence which were commanded by Branko Popovic, Marko Pavlovic and other paramilitary units such as Arkan's units. This attack was conducted pursuant to a plan which was adopted by the Serbian Democratic Party which wanted to take over the municipality of Zvornik to chase out the Muslim population, and to proclaim this territory as a Serbian municipality." That's the position taken by counsel for Drago Nikolic in this case. Do you agree with that statement? I can give the reference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Defence counsel cannot have such a position. Could we please be given a reference? I suppose this comes from a Prosecution statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that. That was Mr. Bourgon on the 6th of September 2007, transcript reference 14934 to 14935, cross-examination of PW 108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I notice that you are alone today, Ms. Nikolic. Do you wish some time to check that?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we proceed in the meantime or do you wish us to wait?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can give her the transcript reference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking the question because I'm trying to be pragmatic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we have a break now so that I can check the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are four minutes away from the break in any case. This is why I asked the question. It would give the opportunity to counsel to check and then you can proceed afterwards. Shall we have a 25-minute break now? Good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I totally object to the question put by my learned friend on page 31 of the record at lines 15 and 16. Mr. Krajisnik has not been invited to provide any comments on the cross-examination of Defence counsel, but to testify to the truth and to the facts and to help the Trial Chamber as much as possible in this case. Further, on transcript page on which my learned friend referred to reflect the wording of the questions that refer to the credibility of witness number 108, his involvement in the events, rather than the position of the Defence of Mr. Drago Nikolic, a party, Defence counsel, in the case cannot have a position. Therefore, I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to order the witness to refrain from commenting upon the evidence provided by other witnesses in the case because this has nothing to do with the facts that the witness has been invited to testify about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. At least it has served the purpose, Madam Nikolic in that you have had an opportunity to clarify. Yes, Mr. Nicholls, would you like to comment or would you prefer to rephrase the question without reference to the position taken or not taken by the Drago Nikolic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question. I think it's fair to comment on a position taken by the Defence when the Defence says this is an established fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let's not comment on that in the presence of the witness. I am suggesting that you rephrase the question without any reference to the position taken or not taken by the Nikolic Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, do you agree or disagree with the statement that there was an attack on April 8th 1992 in Zvornik, the units involved in the attack were the Zvornik TO, commanded by Branko Popovic and Marko -- or Marko Pavlovic is the other name and other paramilitary units such as Arkan's units and that this attack was conducted pursuant to a plan adopted by the Serbian Democratic Party which wanted to take over the municipality of Zvornik to chase out the Muslim population and to proclaim this territory as a Serbian municipality? And I ask if you agree or disagree with that statement.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. And I can't provide a positive answer. I only know that there was an armed conflict. That's the extent of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to go now to a military report. This is P414. It's a large report you've seen before, RS -- VRS Main Staff military secret, strictly confidential analysis of the combat readiness and activities of the army of Republika Srpska in 1992 dated Han Pijesak 1993. I'll just ask a few questions about this report, sir, as the military operations are explained in relation to political goals. I'd like to go first to page 7 of the English, page 8 of the B/C/S. I'm just going to read out a couple portions to you and then ask you if you agree with me on what they mean. This is under the section, "Control and command." First sentence. "In the past year the army of Republika Srpska has evolved into the highest strategic organisational formation of the Serbian people in former Bosnia-Herzegovina capable of realising strategic and other tasks assigned to it by the Supreme Command." I'd like you to keep that statement in mind while I go on to the next section I want to ask you about. English page 69, B/C/S page 62. It's a section --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could this page be put on the screen? I have a problem following you. I can't see the page on the screen. I don't know whether this is the same text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you on video mode or not? Madam Usher, could you check, please, just to make sure and assist Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the document before me, but I don't have the text, the portion of the text that the Prosecutor is reading at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you see section 4.1 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- oh, well, yes, 4.1, yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you need this to be larger so you can read the text? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see it, but it is now only now that it is okay on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you want a hard copy, let me know.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need. This should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. This is section 4.1, organisation and establishment, and it's a bit of a historical section of this report. If we go down to the fourth paragraph, to make this quicker, rather than reading it all: "From the beginning of interethnic conflict from mid-March to 19 May, these forces succeeded in protecting the Serbian people from large-scale massacre and partially in protecting territories inhabited predominantly or wholly by Serbs. However, they failed to achieve the main strategic objectives of the armed struggle of the Serbian people in former Bosnia-Herzegovina." Next paragraph continuing to talk about this early formation. "They failed to open up and secure core through the Sava River valley, Posavina, between the Krajina and the FRY, or a corridor which would link Herzegovina with the FRY via the Drina River valley. They failed to gain control over considerable part of the territory of former BH which historically and ethnically belonged to Serbian people." Now, do you agree, disagree, you can explain or you don't know, that this reference here to opening up the two corridors are linked to strategic objectives 2 and 3?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time, there was a corridor between Semberija and Krajina. As far as I can remember, there was also a corridor between Romanija and Semberija. If you go back to the beginning, when you said that you had mentioned the strategic goals, please read them and see what the strategic goals of the army were. None of them reflects any of the strategic goals from the decision of the six strategic goals. I know that. I objected to that in my appeal. Go back and see what the strategic goals of the army were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we can talk about that, but then last question just to make sure I understand completely, the corridor from the Krajina to Serbia Semberija --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just tell that the translation does not reflect the exact words by Mr. Krajisnik. There are two words from B/C/S, "strateski" and "strategijski." But they are -- they were translated in the same -- with the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what's the difference between the two if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because "strategijski" is the military expression, as far as I understood the witness, but "strateski" is political objective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. But I think, having followed the interpretation upon Mr. Krajisnik's testimony, that's how I understood it, that there was a distinction between the two strategic goals, that of the military and that of the political -- that of the politicians or the political framework. So let's proceed, but thank you for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll move on but quickly. You agreed on the 28th of June or you recalled that on the 28th of June 1992, the corridor was broken through from Krajina to Serbia, correct? That's when the military created that corridor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. On or around that date, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And does that not represent the achievement by the military of strategic objective 2 from the 16th Assembly session, even if you say these are parallel, exactly the same objectives?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying that at the 16th Assembly session, we interpreted what had been agreed with the Croatian side, as to how to deal with the corridor. And you have that in the record. Since it could not be achieved through negotiations, and as a result of the humanitarian collapse in Banja Luka, the military did not because of that paper, not because of the six strategic goals but because of the situation. In order to be able to bring oxygen and humanitarian goal to Krajina, one of the six strategic goals was also access to the sea, but the military did not remain on the coast. They were there but they withdrew. The six strategic goals were a lot of things but they were not the basis for military action. The situation called for the humanitarian salvation being brought to Krajina, and this is as much as I could understand the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to go to page 158 of the English, 138 of the B/C/S. This is entitled, "Basic characteristics of the operational tactical utilization of the army of Republika Srpska." Is the text big enough for you to read?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could this be enlarged a little bit more? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. This first sentence, just going quickly through it, similar to the one we looked at a moment ago: "In the past year 1992, from self-organised units at the local level, the VRS has grown into the highest strategic organisational formation of the Serbian people in the former BH, capable of realising strategic and other objectives assigned to it by the Supreme Command and the president of the Republika Srpska as the Supreme Commander." I want to go to, this is still on the same page in B/C/S but page 159 of the English, and we could scroll down and to the fourth paragraph, please, for the witness. There is no fourth paragraph. It's -- it's a paragraph in B/C/S on page 138 which begins, "This military organisation developed quickly." It's the bottom paragraph, I believe. Now, in here we see: "The strategic objectives of the war were promptly set and Main Staff of the VRS the command and the units served as a general guideline upon which we planned the operations and concerted battles. This means that the objectives were set before us rather than specific tasks spelled out although the president of the republic as the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of the RS did orally assign a number of tasks which were of general and vital significance to our struggle in protecting the Serbian people and its territories. The Main Staff of the army of RS translated the said objectives and tasks into general and individual missions of the army of RS and of the individual operational and tactical formations with the goals of every individual combat action operation or battle being specifically defined." Now, here, isn't this report saying that the army behaved not independently but as it should as an army of the RS and strove to achieve the objectives put before it by the political leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not a Supreme Commander, I did not write support. I cannot help you. You can ask about that, Mr. Gvero and the other generals or Mr. Karadzic when you bring him here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. But you did attend some meetings of the Supreme Command, you testified about that in your trial.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Command was set up as an advisory body, towards the end of 1992. I did attend some of its meetings, but I would not answer these questions because they have nothing whatsoever to do with the six strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what I'm putting to you, you were a member of the government, you were speaker of the assembly, you went to some meetings of the Supreme Command. What this says is that the army carried out the objectives put before it by the political leadership. As a member of that political leadership, is it true or not true or you can't say, what is written here?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not issue any orders. I don't know anything about that communication. Mr. Karadzic knows that. The army members know that. And they can explain how the communication went. And what I can tell you is what those meetings were and what the agenda of these meetings was. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you in Vlasenica with Karadzic just before Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what you're asking me. I don't know whether I ever entered that building or not. I haven't a clue. But I did not know anything about that operation. I know what you're asking me, and this is what -- my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Go to page 160 in the English, B/C/S page 139. At the very bottom of page 159 in the English it starts saying that these are priorities that they are talking about on the next page. At the bottom of the first paragraph of the English: "In the last month and a half our operations have concentrated on the liberation of Podrinje as thereby the strategic objective of our war would be realised. One that could be defined as 'establishing contact with Serbia on the river Drina or the Drina ceasing to be a frontier.'" Now there again, strategic goal 3 nearly verbatim is being set forth as a goal which must be realised militarily, correct? It's the plain meaning of this military report?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see on this page what the strategic goals of the army were. The military did not have a task to break a corridor with military means. At the 16th session we spoke about the exchange of territories in order to achieve a corridor. That was the whole point. After everything that happened, because of the situation on the ground, because of the circumstances that prevailed, all this happened, but I am not aware of anybody issuing an order to the military to act upon any of the goals, and I really cannot see a link being established or how would it be possible to establish a link between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's just turn the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, this is the last question on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Page 162 of the English, B/C/S 141. Sixth bullet point in the English. "By taking Kamenica, Cerska, Glogova, the region of Osmace village and Jadar, the Drina Corps has considerably expanded the free territory and will shortly have achieved the strategic task assigned to it by the Supreme Command while at the same time providing protection for the Serbian people." Can you read that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read it, but I believe that what you have read is correct. I really can't find it on the screen, but, no, I've found it now, but I don't have any reason to doubt what you have just read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If you break this up a bit we saw strategic four, directive 4 earlier, talking about these areas. This paragraph, the plain meaning, sitting in carrying out these military actions the Drina Corps as achieved a strategic task assigned to it by the Supreme Command. In other words relating to your last answer this does reflect assignment by the Supreme Command to the military to complete and achieve this strategic task, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree with you, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, yes, Madam Fauveau, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness said on page 28 that the -- there were -- there are some things on which he cannot make any comments, he is not a military man. So with regards to the comments made by my colleague, Mr. Zivanovic, in B/C/S we have two very different words, strategic words, let's say, when we say strategic tasks and strategic objectives are two very different words and terms. I would like to ask the Prosecutor to put the following question to the witness to ask him if he's ever seen that document and if he can, in fact, make any comments on military documents. Does he believe that he knows enough military terminology to make comments on purely military terminology sentences?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Those are two different issues. Actually, looking at the question and more particularly to his answer, I can't agree with you, "I am sorry," my next step would be to ask the witness whether he wants to explain why he doesn't agree with the proposition made to him by the Prosecution or whether he wishes to stop where he left his answer. And then if you want to ask further questions, you can ask further questions. But it's perfectly legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you wish to explain why you don't agree with Mr. Nicholls or do you wish to -- Mr. Nicholls to pass on to his next question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat the question? There are several questions involved and when I hear all of them again, I will gladly answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I can read it out to you. Mr. Nicholls was referring you to a part of this document, bulleted number -- bullet paragraph 6, and he says, if you break this up we saw strategic 4, directive 4, earlier talking about these areas, that is Glogova and Cerska, Kamenica and the region of Osmace village and the other. And then he continues, "This paragraph, the plain meaning, sitting in -- carrying out these -- seeking and carrying out these military actions, the Drina Corps has achieved a strategic task assigned to it by the Supreme Command." In other words relating to your last answer, does this reflect an assignment by the Supreme Command to the military to complete and achieve this strategic task, namely directive number 4 or strategic 4? In other words, the question is what you read in this document, does it amount to a statement that the military was doing nothing else but putting into execution the strategic goal that was fixed by the political establishment and as communicated to the military for their implementation? This is basically the question. If you wish to answer it, answer it. If you wish Mr. Nicholls to go -- move forward to the next question, we'll do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the fourth objective was drafted, I explained what we meant and how strategic goals could be achieved by an exchange of territories and special ties with Serbia. Because this was provided for by the agreement that we had reached as part of the Cutileiro Plan. I said that everything that happened later on was without any orders. It was never meant for any of these to be achieved by military means. This was not a military plan. On the 9th of June, representatives of the military were present and it was said publish the strategic goals, publish the maps and all that to the international community. If this had been a military objective we would not have sent any of that to the international community, we would have rather said okay let's hide all that, let's cover all this up, so the six strategic objectives were not the basis of any further operations. Whether the Supreme Commander at the time, Mr. Karadzic, did issue any orders to deal with the problems aside from anything else, if this is what transpires from this document, you should ask the military what is meant by that. That's my explanation. And that's why I believe that this cannot be in connection with the six strategic goals, and I also believe that there was no specific order ever issued to do things in the way described herein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, let's move on, please, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to now move to 3346. This is minutes and audio recording of the 24th session of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, 8th of January 1993. This was held in Bijeljina, if you're interested in that. And I want to look at the English page 7, B/C/S, I believe, page 5. It's number 10 is the section I'm looking for. And this is a list of conclusions adopted at this assembly session. And can we scroll down a little bit more? Could we go to the next page, please, first, actually, of the B/C/S? Okay. Scroll down to the signature and stamp. That's your name and signature at the bottom of the page, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my name and my signature and the assembly stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Previous page, please. Go back to item 10. "The assembly has adopted the stance that the Muslims are an artificial communist creation. And because of that, they are not recognised as a people. The Muslims, in fact, are a religious sect of Turkish orientation." That conclusion was adopted at that session, correct? And we will talk about the session in a minute and you'll be able to explain anything you want. The question now is this was adopted, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. 3317, please. Minutes and tape recording of the same session, 24th session, page 94 of the English, 64 of the B/C/S. I'll wait for that to come up. 64 of the B/C/S. And we have a discussion on this conclusion, and it's hard for me to tell where it starts in the B/C/S. There is a portion that says, "What is it, Vjestica? All right. Is there anything else unclear here? Can we adopt these conclusions"? And then Mr. Vojo Kupresanin speaks. I won't read all this out because it's quite a lot of irrelevant text over the next few pages. But Mr. Kupresanin proposes something. He says: "We stumbled over some ideas several times in the past.
