Gentlemen, is this Muslim nation a nation at all?" That's on page 94 of the English. Continuing further in the paragraph, he says: "And yet Bosnia isn't Serb but Muslim of the non-existent nation. Are these not Serb stupidities again. If we make this mistake now, we make an elementary mistake like in primary school. I propose that we deny the Muslims as a nation on the next session of the assembly, no European country or nation in the world would recognise them as a nation and we should take Bosnia maximally. I just wanted to say as much at the end." And then you reply: "I think Mr. Kupresanin is right. I was wrong when I once said don't put them together with us. Because if you push them together with us, we don't know what to do with them. I think this should be corrected a little. We should really take a stand concerning whether the Muslims are a nation. Here we had one suggestion that we say they are a Muslim sect of Turkish orientation because it would then create a discord in the Muslim world, namely Saudi Arabia and some other Muslim countries believe that the Turks are fake Muslims who eat and drink like the others. It's known that they are not so religious." This is continuing on the next two pages, I'm sorry, page 95 of the English, 65 of the B/C/S. Then you say: "Hey, Vojo, you were right and I wasn't." This is still on page 95 of the English. "Let us say a religious group of Turkish orientation. That would be very important to say. Because they are not from any Muslim world but the Muslims of Turkish orientation which is different from the real Muslims." Now, I'm not going to read all this. Skip to page 96 of the English, 66 of the B/C/S. And you say, coming to the vote: "Shall we now take the Muslims out of Serbism forever? All right, gentlemen, can we now make up our mind and take a position that the Muslims are a nation of the communist creation? We do not accept this artificial nation, we believe the Muslims are an sect, a group or a party of Turkish provenance." Then it's put to a vote. You said in your trial you regretted these statements. Can you tell me what you meant by, "Shall we now take the Muslims out of Serbism forever" where you put this to a vote?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I have to answer by way of an explanation. On the agenda of the assembly session, you can also find the Vance-Owen Plan and the discussion was about territories. And it wasn't discussed whether the Muslims were a nation or not. And there were some people who were completely out of control and they mined the entire negotiating procedure. They posed the question of whether Muslims should get anything, any of the territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We came to a dead end and as you can see here, I was trying to explain that nations defined themselves as such. When we were about to vote on the Vance-Owen Plan and the problems therein, I just said, "You were right, I wasn't," to calm him down. The assembly does not have the right to decide whether a people are a nation or not. And I just wanted to say, "Okay, let them be an sect. Let's move on." Everything I said here, well, there was either at the assembly session or at the club of representatives. Now that Bosnia-Herzegovina is being carved up, deputies were discontented and they all wanted to see their small chunks of territory to be on the map. The discussion was about the map and then someone came one this question of whether Muslims were a people or nation or not. Up until the 60s of the last century, the Muslims were not defined as a nation. In the communist times there was a decree proclaiming them a nation. They were one of the parties in the negotiations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for the mention of Saudi Arabia and others, this was all coming from the media, the goal was to stop with this type of discussion and to continue discussing the Vance-Owen Plan. When I said that I was ashamed, I was at the time when the Muslim side occupied my village. That's when I called them Turks, and it's not a word I ever use in my vocabulary otherwise. That's how much I can recall. Either I or most of the deputies, we never said that Muslims were not a nation. However, a number of the deputies wanted them to be proclaimed as Serbs again because before 1960s, they were stating that they were Croats or Serbs which was nonsensical, really. Now, in 1992, somebody had the brilliant idea to say they were no longer Muslims. It was a communist creation let us bring them back to the Serbian body, to the body of the Serbian people. As for Serbia not being able to be transformed and to say that the separate factor, the separate side of Muslims existed, this is not something we tried to deny. And the goal of the entire discussion was not such. You can see for yourself that in the agenda, there is the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we move on and bring this to an end, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to play a video now, it's a video you're familiar with of course, sir. It's dated 21st of August 1994. It's 65 ter number 3318. And it's a large rally in Banja Luka. And before we turn that on, I've watched the video, I've been to Banja Luka, not a long time. This is by the Boska department store, correct? We can wait until we turn it on but I'd like you to confirm that. I'm sorry, it's 3344 is the video, 3318 is the transcript. We can start playing the video at -- it's at 31 minutes 4 seconds:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, there should be sound. I'm not getting any.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just my question, this is in front of the Boska department store in Banja Luka, correct, in that big square?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. If we can play?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we may need -- let's keep playing it a little and see if the sound comes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I apologise, Your Honour, if we could stop here, 3133, when we checked it before and the sound was working. I'm going to have to get a technician to take a look at it. We are playing it out of sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think you can fix this or it's going to keep us waiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I frankly have no idea, Your Honour. We need a technician to come, I think. I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am informed that the technician is on his way already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If it's the Court's pleasure, I'm almost done with my cross, if we could take a break for ten minutes or we could wait in the courtroom, whichever Your Honours could prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's on his way. Yesterday he sorted a similar problem in a jiffy. In a minute it was solved, so I would suggest that we wait for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We can stop for a second. Before the sound was working it panned across some of the people present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, for the record we stopped at 32.012.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that some of the persons presents on the stage were Biljana Plavsic, yourself, Radovan Karadzic, Vojo Kupresanin, Predrag Radic and Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Radic, Karadzic, Plavsic, myself. I don't know whether Brdjanin was there, but I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll see. If we could continue now to counter 48.42? Start playing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay we stop at 49.11.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's Vojo Kupresanin who we have seen in some of the assembly session minutes, correct? I need to you answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We are not going to watch all of this. Let's go to 51.21, please. We can start there that's fine, at 51.17 or .18.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop at 53.27.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The date of this rally, 21st of August 1994, this is after the Ferhadija mosque in Banja Luka had been blown up, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This rally was held on the occasion of the plebiscite concerning the contact plan group. As for the mosque being blown up or not, I really don't know. This had to do with the plebiscite which was subsequently organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe you didn't understand me, I'm not saying the rally is about the mosque being blown up, I'm just trying to get the time and some context. This is after that UNESCO protected monument, that mosque, had been destroyed in Banja Luka, correct? It was no longer standing at the time of this rally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's already told you he doesn't know, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you don't know when the mosque was blown up?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I don't know now, and I didn't know then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, we can continue playing then at 53.27.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop there, 54.58. Move on to you. That's at 1.10.07 or so. Maybe move back a little bit on the counter. Okay 1.10 exactly, can play.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop. All right. We haven't played the whole video but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have stopped at 1 hour ten minutes 36.5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've heard Vojo Kupresanin again saying that there is no such thing as a Muslim nation, heard Brdjanin's infamous speech about wiping the non-Christian filth from the shoes of the Serbian people and now you've characterised these as wonderful words, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a misstatement. He didn't mention Mr. Kupresanin but the prior speakers. And he didn't emphasise the words of Mr. Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Everyone is included, no one is excluded, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, really for the record some of these objections are just simply improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Put your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You remember the question or do you want me to ask it again? You said, "Dear brothers and sisters, my dear people on the Krajina on both sides of the Una, having heard these wonderful words by my predecessors, I feel great satisfaction." And continue. You're calling Brdjanin's speech and Kupresanin's speech those wonderful words, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly this speech of mine was a well-balanced approach which deserves only the highest grades. As a politician first I praised the entire situation and then I responded to Kupresanin and Brdjanin. During my speech, as you can see later, you can see that I said that no one has the right to say that Muslims are Serbs, and I said clearly that we don't hate neither Muslims nor Croats. You have it all on the footage. This was a pre-election rally at which I stood against such war mongering statements and I said, let them live and we should do our own. If one goes into this in detail, I actually denied what they said and I thought it would be crazy to keep the discussion at the level the two of them had used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm almost done here but then this is you taking a stand against the extremists, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said we don't hate Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would it be possible to see the entire video?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My friends can do anything they want on redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move. I think it will be a waste of time in any case, so let's move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 120 -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether he finished his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're 100 per cent right, Judge Kwon, he hadn't finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was, it was put to you whether you were actually taking a stand against the extremists, whether that's what you were maintaining, and you said, "Yes, I said we don't hate Muslims, and Croats." Could you continue from there, please, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also said that what we were asking for ourselves was what was discussed was a peace plan, and I also said that we wished the same for the other side. It was very daring to say in such a heated atmosphere and the time of war. You can find this in the transcript. You can find it on the footage. I also said, "Those who do not wish to be Serbian," and I referred to Mr. Kupresanin's speech, I tried to say something in jest and I said, "Well, if someone doesn't want to be Serbian, let us not drive them away." I denied their statements, Your Honour. I explained this at my trial and I can explain it to you now as to why I approached things the way I did. There were 100.000 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's play the section you might be referring to, 1.22.29.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the transcript as well? Maybe that way I can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can stop. It's at 1.23.25.8.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that the section you were talking about where you respond to Mr. Kupresanin and make a joke?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No it would be good to see the part in which I said and explained everything. Taking things out of the context is wrong. Please find that portion in which we say we don't hate them and that we were in favour of a solution. I explained it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. What did you mean by "we simply want to separate because we can't live together and it would take a war to force us to live together again"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position throughout the negotiations was to be given our own constituent unit that we had been promised. Under that I meant separation. They kept wanting to have a unified, unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina where the majority would rule over us. That was the gist of my speech. Please see the agenda. It includes the plan to recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina and the plan which includes constituent units. The only problem was what was to be part and parcel of those constituent units. That is what I was talking about. There was no mention of splitting Bosnia-Herzegovina up but, rather, how it was to be transformed, and the other side was against it. That was the essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then finally, just go to the end of your speech, 1.25.33.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, we can stop there before Karadzic speaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's the end of your speech. This grand hope that it will all be Serbia, right? In the end.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a matter of rhetoric, very dear to Serbs. However, it was there for political reasons alone. I don't know why you didn't show the excerpt I asked you to so as to put things in the context, to see what the essence was. When you cut it up like this, you're trying to put together a picture which does not tally with what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The whole video and the whole transcript is going into evidence. I will move to put it all into evidence. I have no further questions for you now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Is there redirect? You intimated that there would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to be asking you some questions that remain unresolved after the Prosecutor's examination. Let me start with first things first. And the first thing was the statement about the principles that he showed to you and he also showed you the text that was drafted in Sarajevo on the 18th of March 1992. Can we please look at the text together? This is 1D1156. In answering the Prosecutor's question, you said that after this, there was another meeting in Lisbon, also as part of the talks under the auspices of Mr. Cutileiro. Could you please tell me whether there were any changes with regard to the principles that were adopted on the 18th of March 1992, that I showed to you? And that were valid up to the meeting in Lisbon which took place, I believe, at the beginning of May 1992? Were there any major changes to the principle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to note that this is really beyond the scope of my cross on the map which I said at the beginning was limited to the very technical issue of putting the missing page back into the plan and making it clear that the other map had not been attached to the 18th of March. That's it. So I did not go into any discussion from me about these maps or changes in between negotiations. I just put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You wish it reply to that, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls insisted on the date and he reiterated -- said that it was -- it was the date 18 March 1992 in the principles and the witness testified in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we need this because the witness already testified there were two maps, one in March which is the one he was shown this morning and then there was another one later on in May on which they based the map that you showed the witness yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he testified that one map was the factual findings of the -- Mr. Darvin as far as I understand, and it was not the map created as the base for the negotiation, but the other map was the proposal, official proposal of the European Union.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We don't agree with you, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Krajisnik, could you answer the question from Mr. Zivanovic? If necessary he will repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, let me repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In a nutshell, yesterday I showed you this statement about the principles that you had an occasion to see and you have spoken about it again today. And Mr. Nicholls told you that the date is 18 March 1992. That's when the statement on the principles was drafted. You've said that after the meeting that was held on the 18th of March 1992 in Sarajevo there was another meeting in Lisbon, sometime in May 1992, immediately before the assembly session that we discussed. My question is this: Was this statement on the principles changed before the meeting in Lisbon was held in May 1992? Were there any major changes to this statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try and help you but let me go back to the time preceding March 1992. 22nd of February was the first version of the principles at the Lisbon principles providing the key as to how to establish constituent units and it was said then that it should be done based on the census of 1971, 1981 and 1991. The map was drafted on the 18th of March, showing provisionally the majority population makeup and we said on that day that if we took whole municipalities into account, that would be a mistake. It was said then that even the municipality borders could be altered. We depicted a large area of Ozren with five municipalities sharing the area with 100.000 Serbs in each of the municipalities but they were still minorities. But that's why the May 1992 map was subject to some changes and then smaller territorial units, local communes, villages and municipalities were taken into account, although nothing came out of this. My answer would be this: The principles were not altered; however, if the -- the second map shows that the second element was taken into account because it shows that the principles were not based on the whole municipalities but on smaller units such as villages and local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The map that I showed you yesterday, can we please see it once again in order to avoid any confusion? The exhibit number is 1D1160. Is this the map that was drafted in Lisbon in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was a document about the corridor. You said that in reply to the Prosecutor's question, and this was the corridor that had been agreed with the Croats. Can you please explain what kind of corridor are we talking about and what kind of an agreement had been reached with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you should give me a pointer so I could point things for you on the map that is before us, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it. I hope that you will --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we should place the map on the ELMO and you can point on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can mark it on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, if necessary, we can zoom in a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Can you now explain the nature of that corridor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That corridor would be much easier to show on the ethnic map in various colours, but I'll try and see what I can do here. The Serbian side was supposed to establish a link between these two areas, Semberija and the area around Doboj. That was our goal. We wanted to establish a link between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please draw a line?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm going to draw shows how important it was to establish a link between the two. [Marks]. And the Croatian side on the other side was interested in this part here, because they wanted to link up their own areas, and this is actually the Croatian side here. So we negotiated with the Croatian side because this was a Croatian area and we wanted to create a bypass of sorts, and that was our conversation with the Muslims, actually, the Croatian side. It would be a bit different on the ethnic map and it would really be good to have that map because it would show better that the Croatian ethnic areas could have been used in order to achieve an exchange of territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We have that in e-court, I just offer it to my friend if he wishes to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, let's finish with this one first because we can't have two maps at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, here we see a text in the Serbian language, in the Cyrillic script. Could you just briefly explain the meaning of these areas? For example the first one marked with horizontal lines?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The horizontal lines depict the Serbian areas. The white areas are Muslim areas. And black areas although it was blue originally, those are Croatian areas. And Sarajevo is a separate area that I have forgotten to mention. We should have a separate piece of paper depicting Sarajevo as an extra territorial area under the protectorate of the United Nations and here you can see a separate part which is Pale and this here should have been split between two or three entities once the UN administration was discontinued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark that corridor that was supposed to connect Semberija with the area around Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also it would be good to do it on the other map. However, we believe that this is how it should look. [Marks]. This is Herzegovina, Romanija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't think you understood me. I said a corridor between Semberija and Doboj?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the road, and it was up to the further negotiations as to what the route of the corridor would have been after the exchange of territories. These are the areas that should have been corrected with the corridor. There are a lot of Serbian territories here that would have been ceded in order to have the corridor. You can see this on the other blue and red map.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we have now gone beyond the scope of my question. I was only talking about the corridor that had been agreed with the Croatian side that you yourself mentioned, and I don't think that this is the corridor that you drew last.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is not. This is the corridor that you're talking about that should have connected these two areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please just mark these two areas that were discussed with the Croatian side and the corridor that was supposed to connects them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Croatian side we had agreed the principles, we said that we wanted to connect these two areas of ours. And we said that we would give our territories in Posavina at their disposal and vice versa, and they said we are interested in obtaining several territories in the area of Kupres which I marked here but we did not draw any corridors. We did not reach any agreements. We just agreed on the principles that would be subject to further negotiations within the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have drawn this but now I'm asking you to put a number next to the area that was supposed to be a corridor between Semberija and Doboj that had been agreed with the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I drew up an area, and this is the -- another area. These two areas should have been connected, but the modalities should have been subject to further negotiations. This is just the direction. But this is not a corridor. We should have achieved something through the exchange of territories that would have been subject to further negotiations, and I told you what they were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark by number 3 all the territories that they, the other side, was interested in?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here you have it. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you put number 4 next to the part of Sarajevo that you showed on the map?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the part of Sarajevo. [Marks]. That should have been under the protectorate of the United Nations or under the United Nations administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And finally the corridor that I didn't ask you about that you still drew, can you please mark it by number 5?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the area that should have been linked up. This is it. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I used the term corridor. Actually this should have been an area through which a corridor would have passed.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The exact route was not agreed. It was to be subject of further negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now please mark, but I don't know what number I should use. What is the next number? We are still talking about 1D1160. Maybe we should mark it as 1D1169. I don't think we have that number on our list yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we finished with this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then he needs to put the date and signature. Can you help him, Madam Usher, please? He needs to put the date and his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we can save this document. Earlier on, before you proceed, Mr. Zivanovic, earlier on, Mr. Nicholls offered the other map.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there was an indication that Mr. Krajisnik was also interested in making marks, marking, the other map too. If you wish to proceed that way, we can have the other map brought up on e-court and you can proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would ask Mr. Nicholls to provide this map to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to say that that is not the map. This is the Prosecutor's map. It is not the ethnic map. I have it with me. I can show it to you, and I believe you have it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The ethnic map, you said?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please try going with 1149, 1D1149? I think it's on our list. Is this the map?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I can just explain what that is. That's a creation in the OTP with the municipalities on it broken up by ethnicity which is the same as the one attached to the statement of principles, the one I put in today. So it's the map which was introduced today that was attached to the 18 March principles which the witness said was based on the census and we've just put it in colour and put the municipality lines on it clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the map, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a map that was used at my trial, and I marked it. I can explain what it was about. The basis of what we are discussing now is this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know about this map. It wasn't used in the direct, it wasn't -- it's not just the ethnic census map of 1991. It's some marked-up map from the trial and that should have been introduced in direct. What I've provided or there is the one attached to the 18 March but I think we are now getting into a way beyond the scope of cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can move to your next. It's not going to change anything from what the witness has already stated. He's indicated where the corridor was more or less, and if you insist I think we can proceed but I don't see the utility of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, Mr. Krajisnik, do you wish to give us further information, different, or in addition to what you have already, based on the map that you see in front of you? Do you consider it necessary or not necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that this was a cadastre map with even the smallest territorial units drawn in. It is different from the municipal map. You can see the rural part which to a large extent was held by the Serbs. The blue is the Serbs. And here you can see how corridors can be achieved through an exchange of territory. And you can see why the map of the second or the 3rd of May was the way it was. It was based on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask Mr. Krajisnik to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this map shown to you during his testimony at his trial?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drew up this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has already confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have further questions and another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to enter this map in the records or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not this map, the previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we make a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We'll have a 25-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I see that the family keeps increasing, changing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon. As you know, this is Mr. Predrag Nikolic, who is our legal consultant and we hope his status will change from my understanding to something different by Wednesday, and he's here for primarily the next witness and we thank you for acknowledging him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good afternoon to you, Mr. Nikolic and welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I used to be an investigator with this team, and I have been an investigator since October last year. It seems that I will take on a different role soon. I would like to thank the Court for approving that change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I haven't approved anything as yet. But maybe those are pleasures yet to come. So Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you were asked by the Prosecutor concerning a document, it's 3254. Could we please have it brought back on the screen? He put to you a part of the document, which reads that no personal or collective security could be guaranteed to the remaining Muslim population, and it includes the order that he read out to you. I will not repeat it again. But I wanted to ask you something about a particular part of the order. And that is something that the Prosecutor did not read out to you or I may have failed to notice it. It reads, "Given the growing complexity of the political situation and direct threats on the parts of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic to the Serb territorial forces, concerning further -- a further increase of war-related activities, we cannot guarantee personal or collective safety to the remaining Muslim population." Do you know personally or through some other contacts or information that there were some parts, some threats, issued by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic directed at the Serb territorial forces?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here the growing complexity of the political situation. I have to be honest and say that I don't know what Mr. Klickovic had in mind. Throughout the war, I believe the situation was complex. Therefore, I could only speculate. I cannot really recall what was taking place at the time, if anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This document is from May 1992. Are you familiar with or did you hear about the Muslim forces at the time carrying visible symbols, insignia or anything of the sort which could tell them apart as an army, as soldiers, as opposed to civilians? Did they have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the modest knowledge I possess, what was present on all three sides is that at the beginning, before the armed forces were formed, and perhaps even later, the armed part of the population on all three sides wore civilian clothes. They were all defending their own homes. Perhaps it was prevalent on the Muslim side because they did not have any uniforms. The Croatian side got some from Croatia, the Serbs had some uniforms because of the mobilisation that had been carried out, whereas the Muslims did not have uniforms, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing concerning this: Clarify for us perhaps, who was Mr. Gojko Klickovic at the time, since he was mentioned by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gojko Klickovic was a local leader. I wasn't aware of that at the time. He may have been president of the Executive Board or of the Serbian Assembly or perhaps both. I knew what his position was during my trial, but I cannot recall it now. He was a local leader from the civilian authorities. This illustrates that his approach was completely incorrect. He wasn't a part of the military. Therefore he couldn't issue orders. But people were trying to deal with the situation as best they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would move on to another document shown to you by the Prosecutor, which is 3258. You said that there were some things in this document that were illogical, starting with the header of the document, where it is stated that it concerns the Birac Brigade command, and ending with the stamp at the bottom. Please clarify what the inconsistencies are as regards this document.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 19th of May, as far as I recall, in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the JNA was present there. Before that, on the 12th of May, the VRS was formed or it was at the time called the army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time, this person was a major. He holds a different rank nowadays. At that time, he was probably still with the JNA. Since the JNA left on the 19th, and since the unit mentioned was not formed, he relied on the Birac region, and he called his office the Serbian army brigade command of Birac and further down we have the military post of the JNA which at the time was no longer its designator. He was trying to find his way at the time, and he probably did not receive any instructions from his staff. Therefore, he composed a header the way he did. This is what I can tell you as a lay person. However, an expert on the matter could put it more clearly to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the stamp of the document. You mentioned the stamp. Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stamp strikes me as a bit odd. In Cyrillic letters it says the military post of Sekovic. Usually the former JNA stamps as far as I know were not in the Cyrillic script. The VRS was not organised in terms of military posts but units. That's another odd thing. This is a strange mixture and you have generals and other officers sitting here who can explain it. This is what I can see and it strikes me as improper. As to what it is exactly, only an expert could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next question I have for you concerns a person by the name of Veljko Milankovic. The Prosecutor asked you about him. I didn't quite understand you when you referred to him on that occasion. Was he alive at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was dead by then. He had died. As far as I recall, I was talking about the end of the war. It was a pre-election rally because after the Dayton Accords, elections were underway, and I believe I talked about him then. Everyone around me kept saying, this is a unit, these people were heros, they had a memorial hall for them at which he was the central figure. I knew nothing else about it. Once I came here, I learned the rest. And the municipal representative confirmed the Prosecutor's statement that he was a borderline case, as law was concerned, but at the time I didn't know that. I only knew that he was a hero to them and it was very important for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, Madam Fauveau, will you be putting any questions to the witness or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my colleague does not cover that particular topic, maybe not more than five minutes and if we end today the hearing of the witness, I will not ask for the witness to be recalled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I put that question to Madam Fauveau precisely, Mr. Zivanovic, because I would like you to wind up and conclude your redirect with the witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I noticed that the very last part of your sentence -- answer did not make it to -- into the transcript. I think you said something along the lines that he was defending them and therefore it was a hero to them. Did I hear you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each municipality, in a way, had its own units or a unit, and this is how they named themselves. One of the units of the 1st Krajina Corps, because subsequently Mr. Milankovic was a part of the 1st Krajina Corps with his unit, his unit was called the wolfs of Vucjak. Those who participated in the armed defence of the Serbian people, not at Prnjavor but in other areas were very proud of their own units, in particular of this unit, in which many people had been killed. And Mr. Milankovic led their operations until the time he was killed. Later on he was succeeded by someone else, I don't know when, though. In that municipality they heros. This is what they told me and that is how I referred to them at the rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how he was killed, was it in combat or in some other circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he was wounded and that his wound got infected in Banja Luka. I inquired because I wanted to learn of his fate. And I heard that he died of blood poisoning from the wound, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, during examination-in-chief, you said that 90 per cent of his men lost their lives. If I understood properly.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that was the percentage. Or maybe if not that percentage, I know that the percentage was very high of those who were killed in that unit. It may not be 90 per cent, but I know that a large number of the members of that unit died during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you've mentioned the circumstances under which Mr. Milankovic died, you have also spoken about a corridor that was opened by the military leading towards Banja Luka and that this corridor was used to deliver humanitarian aid, and you also mentioned 12 babies. Could you please be more precise and tell us what this was all about, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and my knowledge is modest, but still sufficient for this testimony, I know that there had been political negotiations with UNHCR and the International Red Cross as well as with the representatives of UNPROFOR in order to allow for the humanitarian aid to reach Banja Luka because that area was cut off. I know that there were a lot of combinations on the table but none of them came to fruition and then a terrible piece of news appeared in the newspapers, according to which because of the lack of oxygen, some 12 new-born babies died, and this was published in the newspapers, a monument was subsequently erected for them. And this broke the camel's back in the political negotiations. That was the last straw. I was not aware of all the details, but I know that there were problems with the humanitarian aid and that these babies died as a result of the lack of oxygen in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing, if you know. Do you know where this road to Banja Luka was cut off? Where was it where the humanitarian aid was blocked? In which part of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the part where Semberija was cut off from Doboj. This is where there was no corridor, and this is where you could not go through. For a while there were air drops which were then discontinued, so the whole area of Republika Srpska was cut off. We were also cut off and there were no communications, and people were deprived of the most bare necessities. That was my information at the time. That was how it was presented to general public and to the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember the map that you marked during the last session, would that be the part that you marked with numbers 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1 is Semberija and 2 Strebava [phoen] is around Doboj or maybe the other way around but in any case, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One more thing with this regard. At the time, under the circumstances, did the army of Republika Srpska undertake an operation and connected the two territories that had been cut off from each other?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say, honestly, that piece of news was published one day saying that the army had broken through the corridor and connected the two and that took place around the 26th or 28th of June, as far as I can remember. I may be mistaken, but I believe that it was around the time that the situation was resolved because that particular day was the holiday of our army, that's the St. Vitus day popularly known among the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to move on. You've been shown a page from the minutes or the record taken at the session of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, a reference is made to the cities which would be given to Republika Srpska, that had had a majority Muslim population before. In answering the Prosecutor's question, you said that at the same session of the assembly, a reference was made to the cities and towns that the Serbs had lost that would remain within the boundaries of the Croatian-Muslim federation, and that had a Serb majority. Could you please tell me, if you remember, which towns are these where the Serbs constituted a majority and which according to the plan that was considered at the assembly meeting would remain within the Croatian-Muslim federation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer your question in principle. In the western part of Republika Srpska, in our Krajina, there are historical ethnic areas which according to that map fell into the possession of the federation, where the Serbs were a majority. Just like was established by the Dayton Accords. Maybe to illustrate the matter best, we lost Glamoc, Grahovo, Petrovac and other towns according to the Dayton Accords, and in the eastern part, we got Bratunac and others that Karadzic mentioned. This was confirmed by the Dayton Accords and a similar situation was outlined in the other agreement in a different form, and Karadzic spoke about the agreement and he said that we could not allow that but at least we got the other things; but in the local situation, it is not the same because people say we don't want others, what others have, we want our own, but it was a compromise that was achieved by the international community and it was very difficult to reconcile local with the regional interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor showed you a video clip with your speech. I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to play the same video clip for the witness, from 1 hour 47 seconds. I would kindly ask the witness to be shown the whole speech of his, which lasts 25 minutes. The video clip is 3344 and the transcript is 3318, from the Prosecutor's list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: According to my calculations, Mr. Zivanovic, if this takes 25 minutes and we have already lost two minutes, there won't be time for a single question after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the option is that we show him the film, the video, and then you proceed with the questions tomorrow or else, if you have some specific part of the video in mind, we go straight to that part and you will have ample time for your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I was not able to take the clips because I saw this video just in presentation of the Prosecution cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What are we waiting for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can stop there, and you've got six minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we hope that you will conclude in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, then, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, first of all I wanted to ask you this. Is this your whole speech? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can see that in your speech, at one point you say that people who are listening to you would vote in the referendum. What kind of referendum are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993 and 1994, we had the so-called compromise maps and action plan and in 1994, there was even a proposal tabled for a confederational Bosnia-Herzegovina which was adopted by all, and the declarations were signed and all of a sudden somebody put all that aside and tabled a contact group plan which was a catastrophe and against our interests, and that's why we organised a referendum in order for people to say whether they were for or against those maps or not because we had been threatened with air strikes if we did not accept that, and finally we ended up with the Dayton Accords which was a true solid compromise after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me roughly what was the result of that referendum? Just roughly. I'm sure that you can't be sure of the exact results.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Republika Srpska, over 90 per cent of the people refused the contact group maps and that's why we embarked on negotiations leading to the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on to the last topic of my re-examination. The Prosecutor touched upon the decision which was issued in your case, and as I was reading that decision, I could see that the Trial Chamber found you not guilty of genocide; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber also found you not guilty of being an accomplice in genocide?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I also wanted to ask you this: Do you know whether the Prosecutor appealed against this portion of the sentence referring to genocide?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not appeal that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's it. I would like to thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Shall we call it a day, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will forgo now because if I start now, I don't think I can finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Krajisnik, we have finished here with your testimony. I will make sure, first of all, you will be returned to the Detention Unit, and I will make sure that the previous order on segregation, which was to have effect for the duration of seven days, or the -- until the end of your testimony, whichever came first, will be terminated. And I leave that in your hands, Madam Registrar. You need to communicate with the registrar. Thank you so much. We will reconvene tomorrow in the afternoon at quarter past 2.00 with a new witness, all right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of June, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.,
